Preserve the fail-closed property from dev-pre-release.yml: if credentials are missing the build aborts before archiving, so an improperly signed build is never uploaded. The path filter that gates the dev build (App/, Sources/, WatchApp/, Widgets/, Package.*, Config/, fastlane/, the workflow itself) ports directly.

needs_redesign.why: `gh release delete dev-latest --cleanup-tag || true` immediately followed by `gh release create` exists to minimize the window in which the in-app dev updater 404s. With no in-app updater, no client is polling that tag, so the tight-coupling requirement evaporates. What remains is a rolling pointer to the newest develop build for humans and for Simulator artifact download.
options: Keep the rolling `dev-latest` pre-release, now carrying Simulator .app bundles and release notes instead of APKs.
Replace it with a plain workflow artifact on the develop CI run (90-day retention, no release object).
Keep both.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 for discoverability, keeping the same one-step delete-then-create so the window stays small and the tag always points at the newest develop head. Drop the 404-mapping requirement on the client side. The 'failed create after successful delete leaves the channel empty' edge case remains but is no longer user-visible as an error state.

needs_redesign.capability: Gradle dependency locking (lockAllConfigurations, per-module gradle.lockfile, resolveAndLockAll)
needs_redesign.why: SwiftPM has a single `Package.resolved` per workspace, not per-module lockfiles, and it pins both an exact version and a git revision SHA — which is a stronger pin than Gradle's version-only lock. The Android carve-outs (`_internal-unified-test-platform*`, `*DependenciesMetadata`) exist for AGP-specific configuration families that have no SwiftPM analogue, and the custom `resolveAndLockAll` task has no equivalent.
options: Commit `Package.resolved` at the workspace path and build with `-onlyUseVersionsFromResolvedFile` / `-disableAutomaticPackageResolution` so a stale lockfile fails the build loudly.
Commit `Package.resolved` and let SwiftPM silently re-resolve when the manifest and lockfile disagree.
Vendor dependencies as git submodules or checked-in source.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, and treat the enforcement flag as mandatory. This is the sharpest trap in the port: SwiftPM's default behavior when `Package.resolved` is stale is to quietly re-resolve and succeed, which silently defeats pinning and would let a dependency-scan gate pass against versions that were never scanned. Also commit `Gemfile.lock` for the fastlane toolchain and run everything through `bundle exec` — that is the second real lockfile in an iOS repo and it is routinely forgotten.

needs_redesign.capability: Renovate tiers and the never-auto-merge set (crypto vendor globs)
needs_redesign.why: The Android never-auto-merge set is expressed as vendor globs over Maven coordinates: `org.bouncycastle:*`, `net.zetetic:*` (SQLCipher), `androidx.security:*`, `org.openminimed:*` (Medtronic Sake crypto). On iOS most of that graph stops being a dependency at all — CryptoKit and Security.framework replace BouncyCastle and androidx.security, Keychain plus Data Protection classes replace EncryptedSharedPreferences, and there is no published `org.openminimed` artifact, so Sake crypto becomes first-party Swift source. The protection therefore has to move from package rules to source review.
options: Port the tier structure and rewrite the negated package list against whatever SPM crypto/DB packages actually remain (e.g. a SQLCipher or GRDB-with-SQLCipher package if chosen).
Rely on CODEOWNERS plus required review for the reimplemented crypto source paths, and keep Renovate manual-only for the small remaining set.
Both.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 3. Keep the exact tier shape — Tier B as the only rule adding `automerge`, expressed all-negative, restricted to patch/minor; Tier D rules placed after it so `labels` last-wins and none adds automerge; groups scoped to patch/minor with manual coordinates excluded by name. Then add CODEOWNERS entries and a required-review rule on /Sources/Crypto/, /Sources/Persistence/, and the driver trees, because the crypto that Renovate used to guard is now code the project writes. Preserve the deliberate safe-fail: if Renovate's swift manager does not report the depType the Tier B rule matches on, Tier B matches nothing and everything falls to manual review — verify this empirically before going live, since the swift manager's depTypes differ from gradle's.

needs_redesign.capability: License policy gate on redistributed dependencies (cash/licensee)
needs_redesign.why: There is no maintained SwiftPM equivalent of the licensee Gradle plugin. The policy content still applies verbatim and matters more, not less: the app is GPL-3.0-only, the whole fork-and-build distribution model exists to keep that workable, and EPL-1.0 must stay deliberately absent from the allowlist because the FSF treats it as GPLv3-incompatible for a combined distributed work.
options: LicensePlist (mono0926/LicensePlist) to enumerate resolved SPM packages and extract LICENSE files, plus a small repo-owned gate script enforcing the SPDX allowlist.
`swift package show-dependencies --format json` to enumerate, ScanCode Toolkit or the `reuse` tool to identify licenses, plus the same gate script.
FOSSA or a commercial SCA service.
No gate; manual review at dependency-add time.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 for enumeration plus a project-owned allowlist JSON and gate script, falling back to option 2's ScanCode where a package's license is not machine-readable. Carry the allowlist over unchanged (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ICU, SAX-PD, SAX-PD-2.0, plus URL-matched GPL-3.0 for the project's own text), keep EPL-1.0 out, and keep the per-version `allowDependency`-with-a-`because`-reason pattern so a version bump re-raises the judgement. Option 4 is not acceptable — this is a legal-compliance gate, not a hygiene gate.

needs_redesign.capability: Dependency CVE scanning (osv-scanner over Gradle lockfiles)
needs_redesign.why: osv-scanner's Gradle lockfile parser and OSV.dev's Maven advisory coverage have no equal on the Swift side. OSV.dev does carry a Swift package ecosystem, but advisory volume for SwiftPM is a small fraction of Maven's, and `Package.resolved` parsing is not on par with the Gradle lockfile path. A one-for-one tool swap would produce a gate that is green because it sees nothing.
options: GitHub Dependency graph + Dependabot alerts, which support Swift/SwiftPM, as the alerting spine, with Dependabot security updates enabled.

osv-scanner over `Package.resolved` and `Gemfile.lock` where it parses, keeping `--no-ignore` so a lockfile can never be silently dropped while the gate stays green, and failing closed on scanner error.
Both, plus a documented quarterly manual review of the (small) third-party package list.
A commercial SCA product with Swift support.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 3. Keep the Android gate's two best properties: fail closed when the scanner itself errors, and `--no-ignore` so `--recursive` cannot skip a lockfile behind .gitignore. Keep osv-scanner.toml's discipline — no active suppressions, and any suppression requires a written reason plus an `ignoreUntil` forcing re-evaluation. Explicitly record in the PRD that Swift SCA coverage is weaker than the Android baseline, and compensate by minimizing third-party packages (prefer Apple frameworks) and retaining the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` soak as the primary supply-chain defense, exactly as documented on Android.

needs_redesign.capability: Security Scan Gate (Semgrep p/kotlin + p/java + p/secrets over Kotlin/Java sources)
needs_redesign.why: Named explicitly because it is the most likely thing to be mis-ported. Semgrep's `p/kotlin` and `p/java` rulesets produce exactly zero findings on Swift — a naive port yields a gate that is permanently, meaninglessly green over the entire application. Semgrep does support Swift as a language, but the registry's Swift rule coverage is thin next to the Kotlin and Java packs. Only `p/secrets` is language-agnostic and ports directly.
options: CodeQL with the `swift` language pack and the `security-extended` query suite, run on a macOS runner, as the SAST gate of record.

Semgrep with Swift rules plus project-authored rules (ban NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, ban kSecAttrAccessibleAlways / kSecAttrAccessibleAlwaysThisDeviceOnly, ban hardcoded keys and tokens, require HTTPS URL construction, ban `try!` around crypto and keychain calls, ban logging of glucose/identifier values).
SwiftLint with `--strict` plus custom rules — lint and correctness, not SAST.
gitleaks or TruffleHog for secrets, in addition to or instead of p/secrets.
MobSF static analysis over an unsigned archive.
needs_redesign.recommendation: CodeQL Swift `security-extended` as the blocking gate (option 1) — it is the only true dataflow SAST for Swift and is free for public repositories — plus project-authored Semgrep Swift rules (option 2) for the app-specific bans, plus gitleaks over the full history (option 4) alongside the existing org-wide GitGuardian. SwiftLint `--strict` replaces `lintDebug` in the build gate, not the security gate. Keep the Android gate policy verbatim: block on HIGH/ERROR only, surface WARNING non-blocking, surface unparseable files as a warning so silently-skipped findings leave a signal, and fail closed when the scanner exits with an internal error.

needs_redesign.capability: Build gate: unit tests, lint, and instrumented/emulator tests (android.yml)
needs_redesign.why: The shape survives but the runner class and the coverage boundary change materially. Everything moves to macOS runners at roughly a 10x minute multiplier for private repos, the KVM/AVD machinery disappears, and — decisively — Core Bluetooth does not exist in the iOS Simulator, so no Simulator-run test can exercise any BLE code path. The Android instrumented lane could at least boot a device image.
options: `xcodebuild test` against iOS Simulator and watchOS Simulator destinations for everything non-BLE; BLE covered by an in-process simulated pump driver plus manual hardware validation.

Factor pure-Swift protocol parsing, framing, and safety-limit logic into platform-agnostic SwiftPM targets tested with `swift test` on Linux runners (fast and free), keeping only UI and framework-bound tests on macOS.
Self-hosted macOS runner with a physical iPhone attached for BLE integration tests.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Options 1 and 2 together. Option 2 materially cuts macOS minutes and gives the lead a fast local loop; it also matches the compile-time-linked driver architecture, where a driver is a Swift module whose parsing layer has no Core Bluetooth dependency. Option 3 is not viable given the hardware distribution (lead has no iPhone; the hardware maintainer's devices are not CI infrastructure). The aggregate 'iOS Gate' required check keeps the same single-status design as 'Android Gate'. State plainly in the gate's own output that it does not cover BLE.

needs_redesign.capability: Build-time toolchain and flags (Gradle wrapper, AGP, buildTypes, BuildConfig fields)
needs_redesign.why: Every mechanism changes even though every capability survives. Gradle wrapper + gradle-wrapper.properties + wrapper checksum verification becomes Xcode version selection, for which there is no checksum-verifiable equivalent — you trust the runner image. buildTypes become xcconfig-driven build configurations. BuildConfig fields become Info.plist keys via `$(VAR)` substitution or `SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS` flags.
options: Committed `.xcode-version` plus `sudo xcode-select -s` in CI and `xcodes`/`mise` locally; Debug/Release xcconfigs; Info.plist substitution for string values and `-D` conditions for booleans.
Xcode's automatic 'latest stable' selection on the runner image, unpinned.
Bazel or Tuist for a hermetic build.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1. Pin the Xcode version in-repo and assert at build start that the selected version matches, because an unpinned Xcode bump can silently change signing, entitlement defaults, and SwiftPM resolution. Map the flags directly: UPDATE_CHANNEL -> an Info.plist channel string; DEV_BUILD_NUMBER -> CFBundleVersion (no separate field needed); MEDTRONIC_DRIVER_ENABLED -> a compilation condition that removes the driver module from the binary and the UI, which is stronger than Android's runtime kill switch and matches the compile-time-linked driver decision; watch-face asset SHA-256 fields -> not applicable. Note the genuine loss: nothing in the iOS toolchain corresponds to Gradle wrapper checksum validation.

needs_redesign.why: Every command maps to a different binary and one command has no mapping at all. adb/emulator become `xcrun simctl` and `xcrun devicectl`; logcat tag filters become `log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "…"'`; APK install becomes `simctl install` of a .app or TestFlight on device. The `ble-raw` lane, which greps BLE_RAW from logcat, cannot exist in the Simulator because Core Bluetooth is absent there.
options: Rewrite as `scripts/ios-dev.sh` over simctl/devicectl/log, keeping the same verb structure (devices, build, sim start/stop/install, phone logcat, watch logcat).
Adopt fastlane lanes for the same operations.
Both: a thin shell wrapper that shells out to fastlane and simctl.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, keeping the same ergonomics and `set -euo pipefail` discipline, plus a paired-simulator helper (`simctl pair` an iPhone and an Apple Watch simulator, boot both, install both apps) since the lead validates the watch app exclusively in the Simulator. Replace the `ble-raw` lane with a `sim-driver` lane that drives the in-process simulated pump driver and streams its log subsystem, and label it in the script's own help text as not-real-BLE. Replace shell.nix with a Brewfile or mise.toml plus `.xcode-version` — nixpkgs cannot provision Xcode.

needs_redesign.capability: Per-user identifier and entitlement provisioning (new; no Android analogue)
needs_redesign.why: Android needs no per-user registration: an applicationId is a string and a keystore is a local file. On iOS, App IDs are globally unique across every Apple Developer account, so two independent forkers cannot both own the same bundle identifier, and App Groups, keychain access groups, and every entitlement must be registered with Apple before a profile can be issued. Nothing in the Android repo prepares for this and it is the single largest new setup burden.
options: A fastlane `add_identifiers` lane run once per user that creates the App IDs (host app, watch app, widget/complication extension, any app-group container) with $(TEAMID)-templated identifiers and enables the required capabilities.
Manual step-by-step registration in the Apple Developer portal, documented.
A single project-owned App ID prefix that users share.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1, mirroring the Loop Browser Build model, with option 2 as fallback documentation. Option 3 is impossible — Apple does not permit it. Template every identifier on `$(DEVELOPMENT_TEAM)`. The lane must enable exactly the capabilities the app needs (App Groups, HealthKit if used, Background Modes for bluetooth-central, Time Sensitive Notifications) and must report clearly which capabilities Apple cannot auto-grant — notably `com.apple.developer.usernotifications.critical-alerts`, which requires a per-team application to Apple and is rarely approved for individuals. The build must never hard-depend on an entitlement a user cannot obtain.

needs_redesign.capability: Build freshness and distribution lifecycle (new; replaces the in-app update channel)
needs_redesign.why: TestFlight builds expire 90 days after upload and stop launching. On Android the in-app updater kept users current; on iOS the user's own CI is the only thing that can. This is the honest functional replacement for the entire AppUpdateChecker/dev-latest mechanism and it has no Android counterpart, so it will be missed if it is not written down as a requirement.
options: Scheduled workflow in each fork that rebuilds and re-uploads monthly, plus manual `workflow_dispatch`.
Rely on the user noticing the expiry and rebuilding manually.
In-app countdown and notification only, with no automation.
needs_redesign.recommendation: Option 1 plus option 3's in-app surfacing. Ship the scheduled rebuild workflow in the template so it exists in every fork by default, and have the app display its own build date, expiry date, and days remaining, with a local notification as expiry approaches. Additionally keep a passive upstream-version notice: the app knows the tag/SHA it was built from and can query the upstream GitHub Releases API to say 'a newer release exists — re-run your build workflow', deep-linking to TestFlight via `itms-beta://`. That notice must never download or execute code.

impossible.capability: In-app phone update channel client (AppUpdateChecker: download APK, hand to package installer, self-update)
impossible.why: iOS has no user-invocable package installer and no sideload path for a normal Apple Developer Program account. There is no equivalent of `Intent.ACTION_VIEW` with `application/vnd.android.package-archive`, no FileProvider handoff to an installer, and no 'install unknown apps' permission. `itms-services://` over-the-air installation requires an Apple Developer *Enterprise* Program membership, which requires 100+ employees and whose terms forbid distribution outside the organization — not available to this project or to individual users. App Store review guideline 2.5.2 independently forbids an app downloading and executing code. Every downstream detail (the anchored `^GlycemicGPT-(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)-release\.apk$` selector, `matches.singleOrNull()`, the expectedVersion-equals-tag check, `parseDevRunNumber`, the 403/404 message mapping) has no target to attach to.
impossible.closest_alternative: TestFlight is the update mechanism. Users enable TestFlight's automatic-update toggle and receive whatever their own CI uploads. The app keeps a read-only version *notifier*: it knows the tag and short SHA it was built from, queries the upstream GitHub Releases API for the newest release, and if that is newer shows a non-blocking notice with a deep link to TestFlight (`itms-beta://`). Preserve the two safety properties of the Android selector in the new context: the notice must state the exact version it is comparing against (no ambiguous match), and it must fail silent rather than fail wrong when the API is unreachable or rate-limited.

impossible.capability: APK download hardening (HTTPS enforcement in code, github.com/objects.githubusercontent.com host allowlist, filename sanitization, expected-size verification, cache-dir cleanup)
impossible.why: This is defense-in-depth around a code-execution path that does not exist on iOS. With no downloadable installable artifact, there is no download to harden, no cacheDir/apk_updates or wear_apk_updates to purge, no filename to sanitize, and no size check to perform. The 100 MB `MAX_DOWNLOAD_SIZE_BYTES` cap likewise has nothing to cap. Retaining the code as-is would be dead code implying a protection that is not being exercised.
impossible.closest_alternative: Apple's own signing and delivery chain is the replacement trust anchor: TestFlight serves only builds signed by the user's Apple Distribution certificate and validated by App Store Connect. Carry the *principles* to the surfaces that do exist on iOS — App Transport Security left at its secure default with any LAN/cleartext exception scoped by NSExceptionDomains to the specific self-hosted backend host rather than NSAllowsArbitraryLoads, an explicit in-code https-and-host check on backend and Nightscout-mediated endpoints, and a Semgrep/CodeQL rule that fails the build on any arbitrary-loads flag. Keep the CI gate that asserts ATS was not weakened.

impossible.capability: Wear APK update client (WearAppUpdateChecker: phone downloads a Wear APK and pushes it to the watch)
impossible.why: watchOS gives no third-party mechanism to install or update an app on the watch. A watchOS app is embedded inside the iOS application bundle and is installed, updated, and removed by the system together with its host app; WatchConnectivity transfers files to the watch app's sandbox and can never install executable code. The Android design — a separate `GlycemicGPT-Wear-*.apk` asset selected by prefix and suffix, its own `wear_apk_updates` cache, its own run-number comparison against `watchDevBuildNumber` — has no addressable target. Note also that the Android bug this would import (`firstOrNull` instead of the phone selector's anchored `singleOrNull`) is moot.
impossible.closest_alternative: Version lockstep by construction: the watchOS app's CFBundleShortVersionString must equal the host iOS app's, and both ship in one .ipa, so 'the watch is out of date relative to the phone' is structurally impossible after a successful TestFlight install. The app should still surface watch-app reachability and installed-version state via WCSession (`isWatchAppInstalled`, `isPaired`, `activationState`) so a user can see when the watch app has not finished installing, and tell them to open the Watch app on iPhone rather than offering an update action.

impossible.capability: Watch face artifact publication and its signing carve-out (GlycemicGPT-WatchFace-Digital/Analog APKs, WFF assets, WatchFacePusher, the deliberate exclusion of watch-face APKs from the certificate assertion)
impossible.why: watchOS has no third-party watch face API. Apple ships no SDK for creating, installing, or pushing a custom watch face; faces are Apple's own and third parties cannot add to that set. Consequently there are no watch-face build products to name, sign, upload, or exclude from a certificate assertion, and the runtime tamper check that compares committed WFF asset SHA-256s baked into BuildConfig has nothing to verify. The entire watchface Gradle module, its `digitalFull`/`analogMechanical` flavors, its unconditional debug signingConfig, and its `vcsInfo { include = false }` all disappear.
impossible.closest_alternative: WidgetKit complications in the accessory families (accessoryCircular, accessoryCorner, accessoryRectangular, accessoryInline) placed by the user on any built-in Apple watch face, plus a Smart Stack widget for glanceable data without a face slot. These are signed as part of the app bundle by the user's own Distribution certificate, so they are covered by the same signing assertion as everything else — which is strictly better than the Android carve-out, where the published watch-face APKs were debug-signed. Data refresh is governed by WidgetKit timeline reloads and watchOS budgets, not by a push mechanism.

ios_requirements: A maintainer can promote develop to main with a single command, and that one push fans out to version bumping, changelog PR creation, and cherry-pick sync-back, with the same message-string trigger predicates preventing any loop.

The repository has exactly one version source of truth, bumped automatically from conventional commits, and the iOS app, watchOS app, and every extension always report the identical marketing version.

Every build uploaded to App Store Connect carries a build number strictly greater than any previously uploaded for that developer account, derived so that it cannot regress when a fork is recreated, a run counter resets, or a maintainer archives locally before archiving in CI.
A user can fork the repository, add a documented fixed set of secrets to their fork, and produce a build in their own TestFlight without editing any source file.
Bundle identifiers, App Group containers, and keychain access groups are derived from the building user's Apple Team ID so two independent users never collide in Apple's global App ID namespace.
A one-time setup workflow registers the App IDs the app needs with exactly the capabilities it uses, and reports which entitlements Apple must grant by application rather than automatically.

The build pipeline hard-fails, never warns, if the archive is not signed by an Apple Distribution identity for the configured team, if the embedded profile permits debugging, or if the profile is expired.

A user can validate their signing credentials in isolation — App Store Connect key authenticates, private certificate repository decrypts — without running a build and without any secret value appearing in logs.
A user can re-run their build on demand and on a recurring schedule so their installed build never lapses past Apple's 90-day TestFlight expiry.
The app shows the version and commit it was built from, its build date, and the number of days until that build expires, and tells the user how to refresh it.
The app can tell the user that a newer upstream release exists than the one it was built from and deep-link to TestFlight; it never downloads, stores, or executes code obtained at runtime.
A user can choose whether their build comes from the stable branch or the development branch, and the running app states which channel it came from.

Upstream CI publishes iOS Simulator and watchOS Simulator application bundles for every release and for the development channel, so a maintainer with no physical iPhone or Apple Watch can install and exercise the full app in a paired simulator.

Every direct and transitive Swift package dependency is pinned to an exact version and revision in a committed lockfile, and any build whose lockfile does not match its manifests fails loudly rather than silently re-resolving.
The Ruby release toolchain is pinned by a committed lockfile and every CI invocation runs through it.

A bot dependency pull request that changes package manifests has its lockfile regenerated automatically on an Apple toolchain and pushed back to the same pull request, or fails visibly; the job that pushes never executes pull-request-authored code or hooks.
Dependency updates touching cryptography, secure storage, database encryption, the build toolchain, CI actions, prerelease packages, or any major version can never merge without human approval.
A required status check refuses to let any bot pull request auto-merge if it changes a file outside the set that the build and dependency-scan gates actually cover.
Every dependency is checked for known vulnerabilities on every dependency change and on a schedule, and a scanner that crashes fails the gate closed rather than passing.
Every redistributed dependency's license is checked against an explicit allowlist and the build fails on any license outside it, with GPL-incompatible licenses permanently absent from that list.

Swift and watchOS sources are statically analyzed for security defects on every pull request by a gate that blocks on high-severity findings, surfaces lower-severity findings without blocking, and reports files it could not parse.
Secrets are scanned across the repository on every pull request.
Every workflow definition is linted and security-audited, and every third-party action is pinned to a full commit SHA, with violations blocking merge.
Every commit is developer-certificate-signed and free of AI attribution trailers, enforced both by a local hook and server-side so an uninstalled hook cannot bypass it.
Changed-path and commit-type labels are applied automatically to every pull request and drive both the changelog taxonomy and the dependency auto-merge policy.
Changes to signing configuration, entitlements, release automation, dependency policy, and the safety-critical pump driver trees require the project lead's review.
No build a user runs ever contains a project-owned telemetry or analytics credential; crash reporting is off by default and can only be enabled with the building user's own credential.
The Xcode version, Swift toolchain, and every CLI tool used by CI are pinned in the repository and are the same on a maintainer's machine as in CI, with a mismatch failing the build.
A maintainer can boot a paired iPhone and Apple Watch simulator, install both apps, and stream filtered subsystem logs with a single command.

Bluetooth-dependent behavior is exercised either on physical hardware by the hardware maintainer or against an in-process simulated pump driver, and every CI gate states explicitly that it does not cover real Bluetooth.
A fork can pull upstream changes and rebuild without manual merge work, and can see which upstream release it is currently behind.
The upstream project holds no signing key, certificate, provisioning profile, or Apple credential belonging to itself or to any user.
Compile-time inclusion of an individual pump driver is controlled by an in-repository build setting that removes the driver from the binary and from the user interface entirely.

risks.risk: Fork build workflows execute third-party GitHub Actions with each user's App Store Connect private key, match passphrase, and personal access token in scope. A single compromised or unpinned action in the build lane exfiltrates the signing identity of every user who has synced that workflow — a far larger blast radius than the Android model, where only the project held a keystore.
risks.mitigation: Apply the existing full-SHA pin gate to the fork build workflow with no exceptions; keep the action set in that workflow minimal and prefer plain `run:` steps over marketplace actions; treat any change to the build lane as a security-critical review requiring the project lead; document for users that syncing upstream pulls new workflow code that will run with their credentials, and that they should read the workflow diff.

risks.risk: TestFlight builds stop launching 90 days after upload. A user who does not rebuild loses the app entirely — for a diabetes monitoring app this is a silent loss of monitoring, not a cosmetic degradation.
risks.mitigation: Ship a scheduled rebuild workflow enabled by default in every fork; surface build date, expiry date, and days remaining in the app; fire escalating local notifications starting well before expiry; document manual re-trigger in the top-level setup guide, not buried in troubleshooting.

risks.risk: App Store Connect permanently rejects a build number less than or equal to one already uploaded for the same marketing version. A run-number-derived or otherwise resettable build number can put a user into a state where every upload fails with an opaque error.
risks.mitigation: Derive the build number from a monotonic UTC clock rather than a run counter; provide a documented, never-decreasing offset repository variable as an escape hatch; surface the actual App Store Connect rejection message verbatim in the workflow output so the failure is diagnosable.

risks.risk: Apple Developer Program membership lapses annually and distribution certificates and provisioning profiles expire on a one-year cycle. A lapse silently ends a user's ability to build, with no upstream visibility.
risks.mitigation: Have the build pipeline report days-to-expiry for the certificate, profile, and program membership on every run and warn at a threshold; document renewal in the setup guide; have the app show its own signing expiry alongside its build expiry.

risks.risk: The critical alerts entitlement cannot be self-enabled — it requires a per-team application to Apple that is rarely granted to individuals. If any alerting behavior in the app is designed to depend on it, most users' builds will either fail to provision or ship with silently degraded alarms.
risks.mitigation: Design alerting to time-sensitive interruption level with custom sounds as the baseline and treat critical alerts as an optional enhancement; make the provisioning lane report the entitlement's absence explicitly rather than failing; never let the build depend on it. Behavioral design belongs to the alerting subsystem; provisioning must not assume the grant.

risks.risk: Swift/SwiftPM vulnerability advisory coverage is materially thinner than Maven's, and lockfile parsing support is weaker. The dependency scan gate can be green while a vulnerable package is present, producing false assurance relative to the Android baseline.
risks.mitigation: Run both GitHub Dependabot alerts and osv-scanner rather than one; keep the 7-day minimum-release-age soak with strict internal checks as the primary supply-chain defense as documented on Android; minimize third-party packages by preferring Apple system frameworks; add a documented quarterly manual review of the resolved package list; state the coverage gap explicitly in the security-testing doc rather than implying parity.

risks.risk: Porting Semgrep's Kotlin and Java rulesets to a Swift repository yields a permanently green gate covering nothing, which is worse than no gate because it reads as passing coverage on a required status check.
risks.mitigation: Make CodeQL Swift `security-extended` the blocking gate of record and verify on a seeded test finding that it actually fails the build; add project-authored Swift rules for app-specific bans; keep the fail-closed-on-scanner-error rule; assert a non-zero rule count at scan time so an empty ruleset cannot masquerade as a clean scan.

risks.risk: SwiftPM silently re-resolves when Package.resolved disagrees with the manifests, so a stale or missing lockfile still produces a successful build against unpinned, unscanned versions — defeating both the pinning guarantee and the dependency scan.
risks.mitigation: Build with automatic package resolution disabled and resolved-file-only enforcement in every CI lane, so a stale lockfile is a hard build failure; make the lockfile-regeneration job's failure block the dependency pull request rather than merely warn.

risks.risk: There is no Swift or Xcode equivalent of Gradle wrapper checksum verification. Toolchain trust reduces to the GitHub-hosted runner image and the selected Xcode version, and an unpinned Xcode bump can silently change signing behavior, entitlement defaults, and package resolution.
risks.mitigation: Commit an explicit Xcode version pin, select it in CI, and assert at build start that the selected version matches the pin; prefer GitHub-hosted images over self-hosted runners; treat an Xcode bump as a build-toolchain change requiring lead review, exactly as the Android policy treats AGP and Gradle bumps.

risks.risk: Losing the fixed release-signer fingerprint assertion removes an equality check with no per-user replacement, so nothing structurally prevents a user's pipeline from producing and installing a development-signed build.
risks.mitigation: Replace equality with a property assertion that is equally hard-failing: Apple Distribution identity, get-task-allow false, team identifier equal to the configured team, profile unexpired. Record the check's provenance in-repo — the Android side referenced a runbook that does not exist.

risks.risk: Every user becomes their own release engineer. A mis-entered secret, a wrong team role on the App Store Connect key, or a stale provisioning profile produces a build failure with no upstream visibility and no shared logs to debug against.
risks.mitigation: Ship the Validate Secrets workflow and require it as the documented first step; make every preflight failure emit a specific, greppable message naming the exact secret or setting at fault; maintain a troubleshooting document keyed to those messages; keep the fail-closed-before-build property so failures happen fast and cheap.

risks.risk: Uploading a GPL-3.0-only work to TestFlight is a distribution under Apple's terms, and the long-standing free-software objection to App Store distribution terms applies to TestFlight as well. The risk grows if a maintainer adds another person as an internal tester on their own team rather than having that person build their own fork.
risks.mitigation: Keep the model strictly one-user-one-account-one-build; document that each hardware validator builds and installs from their own fork and their own developer account; do not add third-party internal testers to a maintainer's team without legal review.

risks.risk: The Android promotion pipeline is documented as built and unit-proven in parts but never exercised end to end, and the lockfile-regeneration path is labelled unproven. Porting it wholesale ports unvalidated behavior into a repository where the first real release is also the first live test.
risks.mitigation: Exercise the full promotion, changelog, and sync-back cycle on a throwaway repository before the first iOS release; verify empirically that Renovate's Swift manager reports the dependency type the auto-merge tier matches on, since the documented safe-fail is that everything falls to manual review if it does not.

risks.risk: macOS runner minutes carry roughly a 10x multiplier for private repositories. A user who makes their fork private can exhaust the free allowance in a handful of iOS-plus-watchOS builds and lose the ability to rebuild before expiry.
risks.mitigation: Document keeping the fork public; factor platform-agnostic parsing and safety logic into Swift packages tested on Linux runners to cut macOS time; cache derived data and resolved packages; avoid rebuilding on documentation-only changes using the existing deployable-change path filter.

risks.risk: The Android repository's dependency documentation describes an auto-merge relay workflow that does not exist, and the workflow-security allowlist names it by filename. Porting the documentation faithfully would carry a described-but-absent control into the iOS repo.
risks.mitigation: Either author the relay workflow in the iOS repository or remove every reference to it, and drop the corresponding whole-file entry from the workflow-security allowlist so it does not silently exempt a future file of that name.

questions_for_pm: Hardware validation depends on the maintainer with an iPhone, Apple Watch, and t:slim X2. Should he build from his own fork under his own Apple Developer account (clean under the fork-and-build model, but costs him $99/yr and a full setup), or be added as an internal TestFlight tester on the lead's account (much faster loop, but is a distribution of a GPL-3.0-only binary under Apple's terms and reintroduces the licence conflict the fork-and-build model exists to avoid)? This is a legal and cost judgment that cannot be resolved from the Android repo or Apple's rules.

Must a user be able to have the stable build and the development build installed on the same iPhone at the same time? On Android this was free — different applicationId suffixes. On iOS it requires a second globally-unique App ID, a second provisioning profile, a second App Store Connect record, and a second TestFlight setup for every single user, roughly doubling the onboarding burden. If side-by-side is not a real requirement, one identifier and a branch-selectable build is dramatically cheaper.
